prompt: People in many countries now depend heavily on their smartphones. Why has this happened? What effects does this dependence have on individuals and on society?
essay:
Few technologies have been adopted as completely as the smartphone, and few have become as difficult to do without. The reasons are partly technical and partly social, and the consequences are visible both in individual behaviour and in the way institutions now operate.

Technically, the phone succeeded because it absorbed everything else. A single device replaced the camera, the map, the music player, the alarm clock and the wallet, and it did so at a price that fell steadily while mobile networks became fast enough to make it useful anywhere. Once one object performs a dozen functions, leaving it at home is not a small inconvenience but a dozen of them at once.

Socially, the dependence deepened because services began to assume it. Banks moved authentication onto phones, employers moved rotas and messages onto them, and schools began sending information to parents the same way. A person without a smartphone is now excluded from arrangements they never agreed to, which is a very different situation from simply missing a useful gadget.

The effects follow from that dual role. For individuals, the gain in convenience is real, but attention has fragmented: work reaches people in the evening, and the habit of filling every idle moment has made sustained concentration noticeably harder. For society, the more serious effect is the exclusion of those who cannot use or afford the technology — older people in particular — from services that once had a counter or a telephone line. There is also a concentration of power in the few companies whose operating systems mediate almost all of this activity.

The smartphone is therefore not simply a popular product. It has become infrastructure, and the problems it creates are the problems of infrastructure that nobody planned as such.
title: Why smartphones became impossible to give up
